text:
When I’m in love, my partner is my everything. Everything else drops away. I still try to make some time for friends, but really all I want to do is be with her.

That little paradise is wonderful, but it contains the seed of its own destruction. Part of why it feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who’s fully got your back. This makes you soft and weak, kinda like a sweet treat or heroin. It is wonderful to have their love and support, but don’t let that bring you away from your own self-love, reparenting, meditation, yoga, and other healing practices that keep you independently healthy. Otherwise, you’ll end up blaming them when you feel bad.

So don’t let your world get so small. Don’t abandon your friends unless they really aren’t good for the relationship. And if they aren’t, ask why. Are they bad friends? Are they slyly interested in one of you romantically? Or is the relationship so weak that it can’t handle anybody with an outside view?

You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance. But keep some room to explore life on your own.

For me, that also means keeping close friends, outside therapy when I need it, a mission of my own, separate interests, some connection to community, and the ability to be alone.

Toft also points out that a man can get feminine energy from nature, music, poetry, art, flowers, food, and other parts of life. I like that idea. A girlfriend shouldn’t have to be my only source of beauty, softness, sensuality, and inspiration.

When I’m already overwhelmed and suddenly announce, “I need time for myself!” it can easily sound like I need time away from her. So I’d rather make alone time normal from early on.

And bring each other out into the world. See people together. Go places. Don’t just disappear into each other.

I’m Buddhist, and the early Buddhist texts don’t teach tantric sex as a path to awakening. But they also don’t show serious awakening as something reserved for monastics.

In DN 16, the Buddha talks about people who had died in the town of Nādikā and mentions 510 lay stream-enterers, 96 once-returners, and more than fifty lay non-returners. Those are the first three of the four stages of awakening.

SN 55.24 has an almost comic complaint. When the Buddha declared Sarakāni a stream-enterer, other Sakyans grumbled, in effect, “Who isn’t a stream-enterer these days?”

And when the married couple Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā asked the Buddha how they could remain together in future lives, AN 4.55 gave this advice:

“When both husband and wife are faithful and generous, restraintful, living righteously, speaking pleasant words to each other—they come together in the future, sharing the same desires and living in bliss.”

Marriage, sex, and household life are not automatically on the opposite side from serious spiritual development.

Kim Anami goes even further: she says sexual energy itself can heal you and wake you up spiritually.

She’s also collected a ton of stories from students who say the effects spilled out of the bedroom into their health, work, money, creativity, the rest of their lives. Her jade-egg practice is a preliminary training for the cervical O: pelvic-floor strength, attention, and arousal without needing a partner.

Brad and Pam Keene are the example I really like. Pam says her Kundalini process completed while they were making love and opened into a lasting universal-consciousness awakening. She later helped Brad awaken too, so the marriage itself became part of the path.

In the previous section, I mentioned the divine feminine and divine masculine energies that you can channel to keep eroticism alive. But there’s really something more special about the in-love paradise that Twin Flames (TFs) experience than a simple Divine Masculine + Divine Feminine formula. Maybe a better way to put it, as my friend Cody says, is Yin/Yang, which still has the masculine/feminine in it, but allows for a more broad type of complementary symbiosis since, each contains the seed of the other.

My ex-girlfriend, Malia, (who is currently hosting me in Sênêgal) found her twin flame (I think) in January, 2026. They only talked for a month, but since she started talking to him, they both have been able to feel the other one’s emotions at any time, from any distance, without having to communicate. To the point where if one feels really bad, so does the other. If one is very happy, so is the other, like quantum entangled photons or something. I’ve also had telepathy with some folks, especially my first wife, Bee, but it was never quite to such an extreme as what Malia has with Mouhamed. Meanwhile his family forbade him from being with her, so he dumped her. Not sure why, maybe because she’s 8 years older than him (although she looks quite young). They both try to pretend like they will be able to get over each other, but I doubt it. Meanwhile, Malia’s trying to marry ChatGPT, but she should have picked Grok, I guess. 😅

Note: I am really afraid how many people are falling in love with their AI “girlfriend” or “boyfriend.” But oh well, I guess those folks aren’t ready for a real relationship.. maybe if they would read this guide…

Back to the topic. There are a ton of people who don’t want to believe in twin flame theory because they haven’t found someone they could call their twin flame. That’s fine, and I am not trying to rock their boat. They might be the people who suggest that you should marry your best friend (or “soul mate” in the TF lingo). Then there are the folks who are deep in the TF theory, believing there is literally one person on Earth who is made for you. I’m also not trying to rock their boat. But I do want to tell my story.

I used to fall into the former camp, then into the latter camp, and now that I’ve experienced two twin flame relationships, I’ve jumped into a new camp I never knew existed.

text:
Conventional marriage vows are dishonest, and most people know it. You can’t promise how you’ll feel in the future. You can promise actions if you really believe you’re capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it. If you tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, the passage warns that God will be angry and destroy your work.

Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 are stranger still beside wedding vows: let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil. To me, the extra promise itself starts to look suspicious: if your yes is trustworthy, why does it need another layer?

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I’m aware of until the 19th century, when people in England began citing romance as their reason for marriage. That trend has continued evolving like a snowball until today. But what our ancestors knew was not wrong: You can sign a contract about what you’ll do, but feelings aren’t contractual.

text:
It’s not always possible in that moment to change a defensive posture into non-defensive loving communication. That’s why I suggest setting a time soon with a nice intention, like a ritual. Sober is fine. You can put some rose petals around you or something to build the feeling, or play some song you both like.

By now this probably sounds terribly artificial. Is anyone actually going to do scheduled check-ins, delayed cohabitation, conversations about hypothetical disasters, imagination exercises, not to mention resisting the heat-of-the-moment stuff and continuing your own reparenting practices when a warm body is available to do some of the soothing?

Well, yeah. It is painfully artificial. In a healthy communal society, the couple would have access to witnesses, elders, friends, and other emotional outlets and resources. Most of us these days don’t have that, so we’re trying to recreate consciously and clumsily some of what the wider field would have done without a checklist.

Most of this article is about what to do before jumping head first into head over shoulders. But if you’re already married with children, advice about slowing down arrives a little late.

I wish I had a special method for fixing that. Mostly I learned the obvious thing the hard way: one person can’t fix the relationship (unless they’re the main problem in it).

With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none. I kept saying, “It’s not possible to have a relationship without trust.” I think that rigidity came from trauma and never really growing up.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it. That drove me crazy. Why would she lie like that? She was lying, but “she lied” only named the momentary behavior. There was no strategy behind it, and she was usually quite honest. Looking back, I could have understood the lie in the context of some kind of mental illness instead of treating it like strategic dishonesty.

Some things were less mysterious. They were acting as if the trust problem wasn’t there because they still wanted the relationship. Attractions to other people sometimes went unsaid too, and sometimes got imagined from nowhere. Some people keep a relationship like this going for a long time, just sweeping everything under the rug.

On the other hand, sometimes I was more honest than my partner could handle, which was its own kind of damage. Ask whether both of you actually want to prioritize radical honesty, first. But the other person also can’t keep saying “not now” forever and think that’s going to save the relationship.

This is the time for agape to shine, because the best thing for both of you may not be holding onto the relationship pattern you originally committed to or dreamt of.

When did you two last dance? And not the “we dance around our problems” joke (LOL).. If that’s where things are at, the trust is out the window. Ouch. I know that one from experience with my first 2 wives and K, too. That generally marks the point of no return, so try not to wait for that. Because once you’re there, as my dad explained a thousand times whenever we had a visitor, unconscious resentment begins to snowball, and we feel colder together than alone. Pretty soon, old Romeo & Juliette might get wandering eye syndrome.

Bee and I were once desperately misunderstanding each other, so we called my friend Eshwar, the only friend of mine whom she respected. He told a related story about something that had happened with his sister. Somehow, Bee immediately understood what I had been trying to say. It was like magic.

So, don’t think of outside help as a formal last resort. I think of it as a part of building community when we learn to rely on each other for this kind of intimate, real-life support. It could be calling up a mutual friend, peer counselor, couples therapist, doing Imago dialogue, Restorative Circle, and/or joining a men’s or women’s group. The key is that both people need to respect the person or process enough to hear something new.

What they say is also partly true: “The only one you can change is yourself.” Not fully true, because we do have influence, and changing ourself does ripple out. Restart whatever you stopped doing because the relationship was soothing you: inner-child reparenting, meditation, body practices, peer counseling.

Many people ask this question of honesty, but it’s unfair. Honesty doesn’t produce a certain outcome. It is its own reward. It might repair the relationship, open it, turn the romance into friendship, preserve the family through separation, or show you that ending it is better. Temporary separation helped Bee and I. It also became more permanent, although I’ve always thought maybe we would get back together in a few decades. If the other person won’t look, you can’t make it mutual. Then you have to decide what you can live with.

I think everyone generally agrees that parents have more responsibility to children than they do to each other, since children can’t take care of themselves.

Before having or adopting children, sit down for an imagination session to figure out whether you two lovebirds can preserve some civil co-parenting capacity after a terrible breakup. That’s the actual long-term commitment.

When it comes to stepchildren, even if they aren’t technically your children, they still become attached. If you’ve been acting as their parent for years, it’s not right to vanish from their life just because the marriage ended. You don’t have legal parental rights, but you can stay a mentor or close friend, and hopefully your partner would agree with this. When children have parental figures come and go, it can damage their ability to have securely attached relationships as adults.

It’s standard advice to never recruit children into the adult war. They get their own relationship with the other parent. However, this was particularly difficult during my first marriage, because Ann was very much unfit at the time to care for our son, Bear. I did fight for custody, but, as my lawyer told me, there was no point, because men generally lose. Eventually I exhausted my options for fighting, and I was left with weekly supervised visits.

Ann was brainwashing Bear into believing that I was “breaking his bones” at these visits even though he didn’t know what bones were. That’s when I told him I had to stop the visits before I end up in jail. So it was for my protection, but his as well, because if he realizes one day his dad is in jail because his mom manipulated him into telling a dangerous story, that could really wreck him.

As it is now, he may miss me, but he is well cared for (I think) by his grandmother, and probably soon he’ll seek me out when he gets his own phone.

I know I sound like a broken record, like my dad, but still: It takes a village. The nuclear family, built on parents’ romance, can often be the worst arrangement for children. If there’s trouble in paradise, parents will try to protect the kids by hiding their tension. But the truth is, children absorb that unresolved tension and integrate it into their very being. In a community, romance is one bond among several, and adult stability for children doesn’t rise and fall with it.

Whether to leave and how to leave are separate questions.

You don’t owe it to them to try counseling unless you also owe it to yourself. If you actually don’t want a good relationship with them anymore, go. No amount of counseling will fix something that has nothing at the base of it.

If you love them and wish it could work, ask if they feel the same, and then go to counseling. On the other hand, even when you love each other, sometimes you already know the issue is beyond what counseling could fix.

Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events? I did with both my first and second wives. I took my first wife, Ann, to two counselors. The male counselor eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There’s no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety. We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.

Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it honestly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should have a chance to speak, and good friends shouldn’t automatically validate either side.

I can believe a friend’s experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited. If someone says, “I don’t have all the evidence,” I trust their thinking more. Living in community would help because your friends would not only hear two stories afterward. Sometimes they would actually see how the two of you treat each other when you argue.

If you’ve been there for someone, don’t abandon them in a crisis unless it’s unsafe for you to stay or they’re creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren’t willing to help themself. You may need to arrange other care. That doesn’t mean you have to pretend the romance still has a future.

Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but I don’t think that means hiding the truth about the relationship to save face. Sometimes the truth is abuse, coercion, or serious deception. How much you say, to whom, and how publicly depends on what happened and why you’re telling people.

A breakup can expose things you genuinely couldn’t see while you were bonded. Look at what you contributed, but also try to understand whatever was true in your ex’s perspective, including the conflicts they were carrying inside themselves, rather than one-dimensionalizing them.

Sometimes the easiest story is that they were fake all along. Don’t grab that story just because it makes everything easier to explain, and don’t reject it if it really is the most parsimonious explanation. Ask people who aren’t heavily invested in seeing your innocence. A therapist, pastor, or even a stranger may see the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend. Even the curiosity itself can be therapeutic for you.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don’t use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex’s wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don’t use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, his cousin Devadatta still kept trying to kill him. Looking honestly at your part doesn’t erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, “What would Mr. Rogers do?” (if you’re old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn honesty. But it can help to keep distance for a while until cooler heads prevail. It can be tempting to let them back into your life after a private apology, and especially after a public one, but keep in mind you deserve a stable love. You’re not a yo-yo.

At this point, I can say I’m better off because of what happened with Bee, Key, and H., without pretending every part of those relationships was beneficial or destined. Loss taught me things love alone never would. And to paraphrase Rumi, “You must keep breaking your heart until it stays open.” (The real quote: “The reed must be torn from its bed, cut, hollowed out, and pierced with holes (wounded) before it can channel the breath of the musician into music.”)

From Bee, I learned what it means for me to be really in love. I learned the kind of woman I actually want: deeply spiritual, sensitive, creative, unique, somebody who inspires me and makes me question everything.

Key repeated a lot of that, which is why I fell in love with her. I learned some of the same harsh lessons from both of them: don’t take openness and curiosity to be fully good. They can also indicate that someone hasn’t developed their own sense of self or opinions, or enough inner adult.

From H., I learned that I can be extremely close to someone and feel completely understood and supported without actually falling in love. I still treasure the support we gave/give each other.

Too many people judge a relationship only by the result, so start measuring what you actually learned from it instead. Relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions. The result is not only whether you stayed together.

Romantic love is not easy, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can’t sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!)

A relationship like this is rare, and that’s probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history. One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with Key: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé came from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They’re suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: the relationship is bigger and more important than the egos in it. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we can’t imagine prior. Nobody can command the spirit to remain. At our best, we serve it and listen for what Spirit wants to change. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn’t have articulated that since I didn’t even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But pathology festers when the environment is perfect for it. The dominant culture hermetically seals two people together and calls that a luxurious privacy. It tells them that sealed room should provide all the fresh air you’d get from a lover, family, community, therapist, and so on. Then it treats the predictable failure as privately caused as well, like mold that grows out of nowhere.

The myths around romantic love become real because we co-create them. We act as though jealousy proves love, permanent feelings can be promised, conflict should stay hidden, and the relationship failed if it ended. Then we suffer inside ideas that were never natural laws, and we walk blindly into our first, second, third, fourth, and fifth marriages!

It might be that I wrote this whole article for my son, Bear, who sadly, I last saw when he was about five, right before he was supposed to get the Rosenblum sex talk.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you’re older and find a friend you love in a super special way that makes you want to raise children together. Don’t imagine you love each other just because you want each other. Don’t feel pressure to promise what your heart will feel. Let the love and bond it produces blossom honestly as your hearts sync. Learn about each other before getting too close, and make sure to keep friends and community around who know both of you.

I believe Rumi was right: A sacred relationship will open and purify your hearts regardless of whether it ends.

text:
I’ve used spirituality as a replacement for intimacy a lot because intimacy was simply unavailable. As a boy and young man, I was so deprived of female touch that it was driving me insane. Meditation sometimes helped me cope better with the deprivation, but it wasn’t a cure. I remember once as I was entering into an ayahuasca ego death, I said, “Actually, I really just want a girlfriend.” Right then, the crazy trip abruptly ended, and a voice said, “Ok then go find one.” Nobody believes this story when I tell it.

I don’t believe most people can be truly happy celibate. People generally aren’t so serious about spiritual liberation that giving up sex and partnership for life makes sense. The Buddha didn’t advise everyone to become monastics.

If becoming a monastic genuinely makes you happier and more peaceful, stay. It might work for some very advanced people, or if your sexual desire is already low, or you’re old, etc.

But how do you know what you’re not aware of? Inner-child reparenting and self-hypnosis can help a lot with that, because often the inner child is being ignored while the adult is feeling some kind of liberation.

And if you’re so happy and free, what happens when you’re alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you? Or vice versa for women. Do you feel like you’re losing some control? Are you afraid?

Bhante Gunaratana, a famous Buddhist teacher, tells a story like this in his autobiography. A super beautiful girl at a retreat he was teaching snuck into his room and waited for him in bed, naked. He went nuts and started screaming at her “Get out!” at the top of his lungs. Obviously he was still repressing something, and she was adept at unintentionally uncovering it.

Robes do nothing. I was mildly molested in public by the abbot of one of Thailand’s largest Buddhist retreat centers. In Thailand, parents have very good reasons not to leave children alone with monks. Tibet is worse.

Forced celibacy doesn’t abolish anyone’s sexuality. For most people it eventually sends it somewhere weird. Why wouldn’t it?

Some people become monks for practical reasons too. In a poor country, it’s free food, a roof and respect, and nobody expects you to hold down a job or raise a family. And even where the food doesn’t matter, like in the West, a guy who was a nobody as a layman gets to be Venerable Somebody, and people bow to him.

Of course, he may sincerely want liberation, too. People can want several things at once.

text:
Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but I don’t think that means hiding the truth about the relationship to save face. Sometimes the truth is that you were abused, coerced, or seriously deceived. How much you say depends on what happened and why you’re telling people, and so does who you tell and how publicly.

Once you’re out, you can see things you genuinely couldn’t see while you were bonded. Look at what you contributed, but also try to understand whatever was true in your ex’s perspective, including the conflicts they were carrying inside themselves, so you don’t flatten them into a villain.

It might feel like they were fake all along, since that would explain everything. But check whether that’s really the simplest explanation before you settle on it. It helps to ask people who aren’t invested in seeing you as innocent, because a therapist, a pastor, or even a stranger may see the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend. Even the curiosity itself can be therapeutic for you.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don’t use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex’s wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don’t use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, his cousin Devadatta still kept trying to kill him. Looking honestly at your part doesn’t erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, “What would Mr. Rogers do?” (if you’re old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn honesty. But it can help to keep distance for a while until cooler heads prevail. It can be tempting to let them back into your life after a private apology, and especially after a public one, but keep in mind you deserve a stable love. You’re not a yo-yo.

text:
Before the wisdom window closes, the main thing is to find out whether you are actually compatible. Do you have the same goals and values, especially around children, religion, politics, health, love, and romance? Where do you want to live? Do you both want to find a community? What kind of relationship do you want with technology and money?

Ask deep questions. Conversation-card games may seem silly, but they can help people get past superficial talk and see if they’re compatible.

But asking, “How do you handle jealousy?” can get me a beautiful answer that tells me almost nothing. I’d rather ask what she thinks she would do in an actual situation. If all she can give me is a general answer, I assume she probably doesn’t know yet.

A card game can create its own little high too. If we spend two hours telling each other things nobody else knows, we may feel incredibly understood and close, but that may mean the game worked without telling us whether the relationship will.

You can also bring the person to a party and see how they act, bring them around your family or friends, or take them to activities you enjoy and see if they really enjoy them too. Try doing what you would normally do in your day alone, but with them, and see how it feels. Is it weird? Are they wondering why you do this stuff? Do they look bored, like they’d rather just hit you up later than be with you while you’re doing ordinary stuff? Can you guys be normal together and not just romantic or dating?

See their negative side first too. If there is no negative side, that’s a red flag for fakery. Ask whether the spiritual story they tell about themselves survives an inconvenient PMS afternoon. How recent is the healing story—two months or two years? Jealousy, abandonment, possessiveness, and the “I’m so much better than I used to be” story may not be understood until there is stress and entanglement. By then, of course, you’re stressed and entangled. 😆

Sometimes the only thing I have is a little “wait” feeling. It doesn’t prove anything. But if I’m about to ignore a question because I really want this to work, that’s enough reason for me to ask the question before I keep going.

If they’re nasty to their friends, family, or other people, assume they will eventually be nasty to you. We mostly seem to get attracted to the inner-child part because we’re coming from our inner child and we want to have fun. But you also need to find out whether there is a healthy adult there before you’re too bonded to want the answer.

text:
When I’m in love, I see everything just from the love angle. I should probably admit that before I give anybody more advice.

A friend in my TherapyCircle chat was talking about PTSD recently, and I said, “I have anti-PTSD.” I coined it as a joke, but even though it feels nice to have Anti-PTSD, it can leave me at more risk than if I had PTSD. Instead of expecting danger, I keep expecting each new woman and each new situation to finally be the beautiful exception. I see the good. I give the benefit of the doubt long after it has stopped being a benefit. Then the false positive resolves into the same old pattern and gives me actual PTSD, like Ping Pong.

I grew up assuming the best of everybody because that’s what my parents taught me. Now I’m trying to be more suspicious and check for red flags before I’m alone with somebody I badly want to please. Why does she contact me only sometimes? What’s the pattern? Is she communicating enough for me to really know her interest level and what’s underneath it? Would my twin flame behave like this? That’s my question. Not everybody is searching for somebody who will naturally channel the divine in their presence.

My second marriage to Bee is the clearest example. I knew within a week of her visiting that she saw me as her father. I didn’t know where that might lead, and it seemed like the only avenue to her heart, so I went with it.

That dynamic alone isn’t necessarily the main problem: a lot of women have seen me that way. The question is whether they can hold it lightly, playfully, and curiously, or whether it turns into something all-enveloping, and they start taking everything they feel about their dad out on me as if I’m him. With Bee, the main issues were the BPD and that her aunts had badly witchcrafted her as a child. She would tell you the same.

She loved me openly and intensely and seemed to understand me spiritually. Most of all, there was the forest-and-mansion line I mentioned earlier that made it feel unconditional. Best drug I ever had.

I don’t know whether that unconditional love ended up being true. I think it was true in a part of her, and it may also have been the BPD idealization. You have to look at everything from multiple angles. But when you’re in love, you see everything from the love angle. That’s the reality shift I’m talking about. It’s great if the ground underneath is prepared for it. If the rose-colored glasses go on when you’re with the wrong person, they make it even harder to understand what’s real.

So I became the father in a relationship where I wanted an equal. Part of what happened may have been that she eventually grew up, and a daughter who grows up leaves home. That wasn’t the whole story. The two years in-between contained enough insanity for several lifetimes.

Looking back, I’m grateful I loved her. For three months after we broke up, I trained myself to replace missing her with loving her, and now, any time I think of her, I feel so much joy and love, which I send her way.

That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.

text:
In ordinary life, I sometimes think of the woman as the engine and myself as the steering wheel, and I get motivation from her. She is the life force. She brings inspiration, beauty, intuition, creativity, and this feeling that life is worth doing.

I help give it direction and make it operational.

I find the intuitive mind incredibly sexy, because I can’t fully follow it. During sex, some of the most “womanly” women I’ve loved have gone through psychic experiences, memories that felt like past lives, and things I had no idea how to explain. One time, Bee said she almost got enlightened, but I came too fast. Woops...

Key could sometimes start talking and somehow teleport me outside the galaxy. I don’t know how else to describe it. Her voice would become so beautiful that I would shed tears that felt super liberating.

Bee could bring out something similar--she could be talking to me for hours on end, but instead of trying to mute her with the TV remote, I felt I was in a timeless dimension of love.

Maybe women are poetry and men are prose.

Some women barely have that poetic quality, and artistic men can live much closer to it. I’m referring more to feminine vs masculine archetypes. What attracts me is the feminine intuitive leap, because it’s hard for me to understand, seems often absurd, yet many times may turn out more accurate than what I could have figured. I hope this feminine quality can be treasured by all girls as they grow, without falling into helplessness or chaos that over-relying on it without calibration could create. Boys should also maintain their access to this, even if it’s not primary.

This polarity is attracting, but it also shows up in arguments. Toft says that after fifty years of marriage, sometimes his wife wants to talk while he wants to fix, a la Men are From Mars, Women are from Venus. I recognize that as well. So I ask, “Do you want me to help figure this out, or do you mostly want me to listen?” Listening doesn’t mean I’m gonna be a doormat tho. If I start listening to her demonize me, that’s the Crucible safety problem I already talked about.

Where I like the polarity is when she sees the Big Picture, and I help fill in the details to make our plan workable. If she micromanages, I start feeling useless. If she earns more than me, although that’s not inherently problematic, it often becomes so, because she will naturally start to feel like she is the one who should make the decisions (”My house, my rules”).

She may know much more than I do about some particular field, including a traditionally non-feminine one, and in that case I want her help. “Honey, let me help you with this,” can be very sexy, until helping turns into doing everything for me and I start feeling useless.

In my experience, women often prefer me to say directly:

“This is where I want to go. This is what I think we should do. Are you game?”

She might have a better idea, or just not want to do it, but she still wants me to take initiative.

I don’t think equality means dividing every role 50/50. If I like driving and she likes cooking, great. If she’s way better at something, she’ll probably do more of it. When I’m leading, I still want to know what she sees. Mandar obedeciendo—Lead by following—as the Zapatistas say.

These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

text:
Here’s the funny thing many people don’t understand: labels don’t create commitment, but they can still expose whether two people think they’re in the same relationship, which matters a lot.

True commitment grows out of relational depth, not a label: if we spend hours telling each other our deepest longings, fears, and problems, I’ll naturally be ready to help when you need me. I don’t need to promise that on paper. If someone says “I love you, I feel you, I’m here for you,” yet they hardly ever talk to you about what matters, that’s a red flag.

The person getting more of what they want may think the arrangement is fulfilling. Usually they’re just less aware that it isn’t. In college I had a friend with four girlfriends who boasted about it to girls while trying to get a fifth. I asked him, “But are you really happy?” He said, “No, I’m miserable, dude. I feel empty inside.”

The full conversation is so big that almost nobody would have casual sex if they took it seriously. Which is why almost nobody has the full conversation. I can’t decide what is okay for anybody else. I can say that most people who defend casual sex are not being very honest with themselves about pregnancy, attachment, or what they might owe the person afterward.

Outside a loving poly community or tribe, I think honest casual sex is almost impossible. If you want something closer to “casual love-making” without quite so many ways to damage each other, you probably need to find a free-love community where the people aren’t disposable, the bonds can be acknowledged, and any children have a village. But if the community is specifically designed to prioritize free love, you might find it attracts people who have traumas that produce trouble with connecting deeply, as ex-Tamera leader, Martin Winiecki wrote about after leaving recently.

This is a horrible catch-22. Wounded people get lonely, and loneliness itself can kill. But the wounds that make somebody desperate for a relationship may also make them a terrible person to be in one with. People don’t only trigger each other and learn lessons. Sometimes they terrorize or kill each other.

I’m pretty conservative about this. I would tell most of my friends not to date yet. First love your inner child. If you can’t even do that, forget a relationship for now. Get a cat or a puppy. If you’re dishonest, can’t care what happens to another person, or keep turning every relationship into the same disaster, come on. You’re not ready.

You don’t have to be completely healed, but the present-day adult has to be able to parent whatever intimacy wakes up inside you, and responsible enough to deal with an actual child if sex creates one. If you can’t be a parent in either sense, you aren’t ready to date.

A good relationship can teach you self-love too, which is part of the problem: you may need one most when you’re least capable of creating a good one, recognizing one, or keeping it good. It depends what each of you are ready for and have the resources for. Here’s a video that can help understand the long process.

These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.

If only the serious attractions are supposed to be disclosed, each disclosure becomes such a major event that people are less likely to say anything at all, so I would rather make every attraction possible to mention casually, including the low-stakes ones.

People promise a foundational, permanent, exclusive romantic partnership far more often than they actually live one. In a polyamorous relationship the boundaries might be more negotiable, but that actually means negotiating is required.

Polyamory isn’t automatically better, though, because it can be dishonest too. These days, I believe it is often a way to cope with an inability to connect deeply with one person, or a way to admit a lack of self-control without necessarily doing the self-development that would make the arrangement ethical. Sometimes pretending to be monogamous does more damage than an outside connection would have, so if you can’t do monogamy, it’s still more honest to say so.

I learned most of this by screwing it up, and some of it I just thought through, so I’m still not sure about all of it.

And then there’s the situationship, which is hard to define because that’s basically the point. Usually it’s a happenstance relationship based on sex. There’s less communication, and what communication exists is more superficial. Yet it is obviously some kind of relationship even while one or both people refuse to name it. It can go either way, but often the man wants to keep it undefined while the woman wants commitment, partly because she’s the one risking pregnancy. Whoever keeps it undefined gets the fun without (most of) the responsibility. But people still get pregnant and attached, whatever they call it. The one keeping it that way still ends up with the existential void another superficial fix creates. Doomscrolling entertains you too.

text:
While different maturity levels are to be expected to some degree, it can get out of hand at the extremes. What I noticed in all of my most intimate relationships was that when one person was always the child and the other is always the therapist, guru, doctor, or dad, then it’s too unequal, and eventually there will be some kind of pendulum swing or backlash. When I became consistently the responsible one, that also made me responsible for everything that went wrong, not to mention the unhealthy clinginess, jealousy, and all the rest which went along with that dynamic.

Toft says, “She’s not a girl,” and “She’s not your mother.” I agree with the warning, but I’d qualify the first sentence. A lot of women enjoy a daddy/little-girl dimension with a man they trust, and I don’t see a reason to deny them that. It can be affectionate, erotic, comforting, or playful.

The problem is when the role takes over the relationship. She can be my little girl sometimes without becoming my child. She still has to remain responsible for her life and keep reparenting herself.

It can run the other way too. If she has to calm me down every time I’m upset, and on top of that organize my life and keep me functional, then I’ve made her Mom.

All three women told me at some point that they felt like my patient, and I couldn’t exactly argue with them. They asked me about almost every medical, mental-health, and practical problem:

“I’m sick. What should I take?”

“I’m sad. What should I do?”

I usually had some idea, so of course I answered, but enough moments become a pattern.

Key at first asked me innocently, “Can you be my guru?” I told her, “I’m not anyone’s guru, but we can learn from each other.” A few months later, she was telling me she was much more spiritually advanced than me. I asked, “Do you recall asking me to be your guru?” She said, “Wow, I must have been really confused back then!”

I also have to admit, I can become condescending when somebody stops taking responsibility for their behavior. I find that intolerable. If someone tells me, “I feel like your patient,” we both have to look at what we’re doing.

I know what happens on my side. Helping feels good, and so does being needed. A lot of the time I really did have the answer or the perspective they needed, so of course they kept asking me. I also had to look at whether they were trying to take care of themselves without me.

text:
A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? I can hear a whole future in those two words—sex, exclusivity, living together, money, children, caregiving. She might mean, “We really like each other; let’s see what happens.” I actually like letting a relationship flow with some parts left unnamed, but the problem is when we’re using the same words for two different futures.

Sometimes what two people want is much more practical. They want to share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, maybe have sex, and not pretend all of that depends on overwhelming romantic love. I’d call that a practical partnership. There’s nothing inherently wrong with that arrangement if both people know that’s what they’re doing. But I suspect they simply have never been in love, so they don’t have that expectation. And that becomes a problem if they ever do fall for someone.

Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love and want to build something together, and they can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life, as long as nobody pretends they can guarantee what either heart will feel ten years later.

Then the questions change for me. If the romance changes, which parts are still supposed to remain? Are we promising actions, or low-key pretending to promise permanent feelings? Which needs are we still going to meet outside the relationship?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? What counts as betrayal, and what’s just a sign we need a serious talk? If our lives change, can we honestly sit down and rethink the agreement? If we split up, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe our kids, if we have any?

These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there’s real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity. And again, community can make all of this a lot less scary.

text:
By now this probably sounds terribly artificial. Is anyone actually going to do scheduled check-ins, delayed cohabitation, conversations about hypothetical disasters, imagination exercises, not to mention resisting the heat-of-the-moment stuff and continuing your own reparenting practices when a warm body is available to do some of the soothing?

Well, yeah. It is painfully artificial. In a healthy communal society, the couple would have access to witnesses, elders, friends, and other emotional outlets and resources. Most of us these days don’t have that, so we’re trying to recreate consciously and clumsily some of what the wider field would have done without a checklist.

Most of this article is about what to do before jumping head first into head over shoulders. But if you’re already married with children, advice about slowing down arrives a little late.

I wish I had a special method for fixing that. Mostly I learned the obvious thing the hard way: one person can’t fix the relationship (unless they’re the main problem in it).

With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none. I kept saying, “It’s not possible to have a relationship without trust.” I think that rigidity came from trauma and never really growing up.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it. That drove me crazy. Why would she lie like that? She was lying, but “she lied” only named the momentary behavior. There was no strategy behind it, and she was usually quite honest. Looking back, I could have understood the lie in the context of some kind of mental illness instead of treating it like strategic dishonesty.

Some things were less mysterious: they were acting as if the trust problem wasn’t there because they still wanted the relationship. Attractions to other people sometimes went unsaid too, and sometimes got imagined from nowhere. Some people keep a relationship like this going for a long time, just sweeping everything under the rug.

On the other hand, sometimes I was more honest than my partner could handle, which was its own kind of damage. Ask whether both of you actually want to prioritize radical honesty, first. But the other person also can’t keep saying “not now” forever and think that’s going to save the relationship.

This is the time for agape to shine, because the best thing for both of you may not be holding onto the relationship pattern you originally committed to or dreamt of.

When did you two last dance? And not the “we dance around our problems” joke (LOL).. If that’s where things are at, the trust is out the window. Ouch. I know that one from experience with my first 2 wives and K, too. That generally marks the point of no return, so try not to wait for that. Because once you’re there, as my dad explained a thousand times whenever we had a visitor, unconscious resentment begins to snowball, and we feel colder together than alone. Pretty soon, old Romeo & Juliette might get wandering eye syndrome.

text:
Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events? I did with both my first and second wives. I took my first wife, Ann, to two counselors. The male counselor eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There’s no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety. We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.

Many say it’s best to save face and work things out privately, but I’d disagree. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it honestly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should get a chance to speak, and good friends should hear both sides before validating either.

I can believe a friend’s experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited. If someone says, “I don’t have all the evidence,” I trust their thinking more. Living in community would help because your friends would not only hear two stories afterward. Sometimes they would actually see how the two of you treat each other when you argue.

If you’ve been there for someone, don’t abandon them in a crisis unless it’s unsafe for you to stay or they’re creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren’t willing to help themself. You may need to arrange other care, but that’s no reason to pretend the romance still has a future.

text:
A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

“We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? I can hear a whole future in those two words—sex, exclusivity, living together, money, children, caregiving. She might mean, “We really like each other; let’s see what happens.” I actually like letting a relationship flow with some parts left unnamed, but the problem is when we’re using the same words for two different futures.

Sometimes what two people want is much more practical. They want to share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, maybe have sex, and not pretend all of that depends on overwhelming romantic love. I’d call that a practical partnership. There’s nothing inherently wrong with that arrangement if both people know that’s what they’re doing. But I suspect they simply have never been in love, so they don’t have that expectation. And that becomes a problem if they ever do fall for someone.

Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love and want to build something together, and they can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life, as long as nobody pretends they can guarantee what either heart will feel ten years later.

Then the questions change for me: if the romance changes, which parts are still supposed to remain? Are we promising actions (or low-key pretending to promise permanent feelings)? Which needs are we still going to meet outside the relationship?

And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? What counts as betrayal, and what’s just a sign we need a serious talk? If our lives change, can we honestly sit down and rethink the agreement, and if we split up, what do we still owe each other (and our kids, if we have any)?

These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there’s real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity. And again, community can make all of this a lot less scary.

text:
Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but I wouldn’t ask someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” That would be a pretty weird date.

At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones. If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”

“I have baggage” tells me almost nothing. What are you having trouble with now? What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I’d want both of us to be honest about how effective we actually are at handling our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control? How dependable are we? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us announcing that we’re healed.

The most recent conflicts are the best place to look. Were you able to regulate at all during the conflict? What did you do to the other person? How did you repair afterward? What did you learn? Has your judgment gotten better, or do you keep falling for the same stuff? What would your friends or exes say?

And if you tell me you shut down, okay, what does that mean: did you stop talking to your partner for days, and did they feel abandoned?

text:
At this point, I can say I’m better off because of what happened with Bee, Key, and H., without pretending every part of those relationships was beneficial or destined. Loss taught me things love alone never would, or to paraphrase Rumi, “You must keep breaking your heart until it stays open.” (The real quote: “The reed must be torn from its bed, cut, hollowed out, and pierced with holes (wounded) before it can channel the breath of the musician into music.”)

From Bee, I learned what it means for me to be really in love. I learned the kind of woman I actually want: deeply spiritual, sensitive, creative, unique, somebody who inspires me and makes me question everything.

Key repeated a lot of that, which is why I fell in love with her. I learned some of the same harsh lessons from both of them: don’t take openness and curiosity to be fully good. They can also indicate that someone hasn’t developed their own sense of self or opinions, or enough inner adult.

From H., I learned that I can be extremely close to someone and feel completely understood and supported without actually falling in love. I still treasure the support we gave/give each other.

Too many people judge a relationship only by the result, so start measuring what you actually learned from it instead. Relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions. The result is not only whether you stayed together.

Romantic love is not easy, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can’t sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!)

A relationship like this is rare, and that’s probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history. One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with Key: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé came from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They’re suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: the relationship is bigger and more important than the egos in it. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we can’t imagine prior. Nobody can command the spirit to remain. At our best, we serve it and listen for what Spirit wants to change. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn’t have articulated that since I didn’t even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But pathology festers when the environment is perfect for it. The dominant culture hermetically seals two people together and calls that a luxurious privacy. It tells them that sealed room should provide all the fresh air you’d get from a lover, family, community, therapist, and so on. Then it treats the predictable failure as privately caused as well, like mold that grows out of nowhere.

The myths around romantic love become real because we co-create them. We act as though jealousy proves love, permanent feelings can be promised, conflict should stay hidden, and the relationship failed if it ended. Then we suffer inside ideas that were never natural laws, and we walk blindly into our first, second, third, fourth, and fifth marriages!

It might be that I wrote this whole article for my son, Bear, who sadly, I last saw when he was about five, right before he was supposed to get the Rosenblum sex talk.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you’re older and find a friend you love in a super special way that makes you want to raise children together. Don’t imagine you love each other just because you want each other. Don’t feel pressure to promise what your heart will feel. Let the love and bond it produces blossom honestly as your hearts sync. Learn about each other before getting too close, and make sure to keep friends and community around who know both of you.

I believe Rumi was right: A sacred relationship will open and purify your hearts regardless of whether it ends.

text:
Conventional marriage vows are dishonest, and most people know it. You can’t promise how you’ll feel in the future. You can promise actions if you really believe you’re capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it. If you tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, the passage warns that God will be angry and destroy your work.

Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 make the wedding vow itself look even more suspicious (to me, anyway): let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil.

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I’m aware of until the 19th century, when people in England began citing romance as their reason for marriage. That trend has continued evolving like a snowball until today. But what our ancestors knew was not wrong: You can sign a contract about what you’ll do, but feelings aren’t contractual.

text:
I’m Buddhist, and the early Buddhist texts have nothing on tantric sex as a path to awakening, but plenty of the people they show getting seriously awakened were lay people.

In DN 16, the Buddha talks about people who had died in the town of Nādikā and mentions 510 lay stream-enterers, 96 once-returners, and more than fifty lay non-returners, the first three of the four stages of awakening.

SN 55.24 has an almost comic complaint: when the Buddha declared Sarakāni a stream-enterer, other Sakyans grumbled, in effect, “Who isn’t a stream-enterer these days?”

And when the married couple Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā asked the Buddha how they could remain together in future lives, AN 4.55 gave this advice:

“When both husband and wife are faithful and generous, restraintful, living righteously, speaking pleasant words to each other—they come together in the future, sharing the same desires and living in bliss.”

Marriage, sex, and household life are not automatically on the opposite side from serious spiritual development.

The example I really like is Brad and Pam Keene, whose marriage itself became part of the path. Pam says her Kundalini process completed while they were making love and opened into a lasting universal-consciousness awakening, and she later helped Brad awaken too.

text:
I’ve used spirituality as a replacement for intimacy a lot because intimacy was simply unavailable. As a boy and young man, I was so deprived of female touch that it was driving me insane. Meditation sometimes helped me cope better with the deprivation, but it wasn’t a cure. I remember once as I was entering into an ayahuasca ego death, I said, “Actually, I really just want a girlfriend.” Right then, the crazy trip abruptly ended, and a voice said, “Ok then go find one.” Nobody believes this story when I tell it.

I don’t believe most people can be truly happy celibate. People generally aren’t so serious about spiritual liberation that giving up sex and partnership for life makes sense. The Buddha didn’t advise everyone to become monastics.

If becoming a monastic genuinely makes you happier and more peaceful, stay. It might work for some very advanced people, or if your sexual desire is already low, or you’re old, etc.

But how do you know what you’re not aware of? Inner-child reparenting and self-hypnosis can help a lot with that, because often the inner child is being ignored while the adult is feeling some kind of liberation.

And if you’re so happy and free, what happens when you’re alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you? Or vice versa for women. Do you feel like you’re losing some control? Are you afraid?

Bhante Gunaratana, a famous Buddhist teacher, tells a story like this in his autobiography. A super beautiful girl at a retreat he was teaching snuck into his room and waited for him in bed, naked. He went nuts and started screaming at her “Get out!” at the top of his lungs. Obviously he was still repressing something, and she was adept at unintentionally uncovering it.

Robes do nothing. I was mildly molested in public by the abbot of one of Thailand’s largest Buddhist retreat centers. In Thailand, parents have very good reasons not to leave children alone with monks. Tibet is worse.

Forced celibacy doesn’t magically abolish anyone’s sexuality. For most people, it eventually just makes them more perverted, since they have no legitimate way to express it.

Some people become monks for practical reasons too. In a poor country, they're given free food, free shelter and massive unearned respect, without any expectation that they have to hold down a job or raise a family. And even where the free food doesn’t matter as much, like in some wealthy area of the West, a guy who was a nobody as a layman gets to be Venerable Nobody, and people bow to him as he preaches how they can also become Nobody some day.

Of course, Mr. Nobody may sincerely want liberation, too. People can want several things at once.

text:
I’m Buddhist, and the early Buddhist texts have nothing on tantric sex as a path to awakening, but plenty of the people they show getting seriously awakened were lay people.

In DN 16, the Buddha talks about people who had died in the town of Nādikā and mentions 510 lay stream-enterers, 96 once-returners, and more than fifty lay non-returners, the first three of the four stages of awakening.

SN 55.24 has an almost comic complaint: when the Buddha declared Sarakāni a stream-enterer, other Sakyans grumbled, in effect, “Who isn’t a stream-enterer these days?”

And when the married couple Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā asked the Buddha how they could remain together in future lives, AN 4.55 gave this advice:

“When both husband and wife are faithful and generous, restraintful, living righteously, speaking pleasant words to each other—they come together in the future, sharing the same desires and living in bliss.”

Marriage, sex, and household life aren't automatically in conflict with serious spiritual development.

Kim Anami goes even further: she says sexual energy itself, when used properly, can heal you and wake you up spiritually along with your beloved.

She’s also collected a ton of stories from students who say the effects spilled out of the bedroom into the rest of their life, with better health, more rewarding careers, checks rolling in, and creativity flowing out like nobody's business. Her jade-egg practice is a preliminary training for the cervical O, as it strengthens the pelvic-floor while also engaging your attention to the sensations down there. No partner required for the jade egg phase.

Brad and Pam Keene are the example couple I really liked as an example of how her method works. Pam explained that her Kundalini process completed while they were making love and opened her into a lasting universal-consciousness awakening. She later helped Brad awaken too, so the marriage itself became part of the path.

In the previous section, I mentioned the divine feminine and divine masculine energies that you can channel to keep eroticism alive. But there’s really something more special about the in-love paradise that Twin Flames (TFs) experience than a simple Divine Masculine + Divine Feminine formula. Maybe a better way to put it, as my friend Cody says, is Yin/Yang, which still has the masculine/feminine in it, but allows for a more broad type of complementary symbiosis since, each contains the seed of the other.

My ex-girlfriend, Malia, (who is currently hosting me in Sênêgal) found her twin flame (I think) in January, 2026. They only talked for a month, but since she started talking to him, they both have been able to feel the other one’s emotions at any time, from any distance, without having to communicate. To the point where if one feels really bad, so does the other. If one is very happy, so is the other, like quantum entangled photons or something. I’ve also had telepathy with some folks, especially my first wife, Bee, but it was never quite to such an extreme as what Malia has with Mouhamed. Meanwhile his family forbade him from being with her, so he dumped her. Not sure why, maybe because she’s 8 years older than him (although she looks quite young). They both try to pretend like they will be able to get over each other, but I doubt it. Meanwhile, Malia’s trying to marry ChatGPT, but she should have picked Grok, I guess. 😅

Note: I am really afraid how many people are falling in love with their AI “girlfriend” or “boyfriend.” But oh well, I guess those folks aren’t ready for a real relationship.. maybe if they would read this guide…

Back to the topic. There are a ton of people who don’t want to believe in twin flame theory because they haven’t found someone they could call their twin flame. That’s fine, and I am not trying to rock their boat. They might be the people who suggest that you should marry your best friend (or “soul mate” in the TF lingo). Then there are the folks who are deep in the TF theory, believing there is literally one person on Earth who is made for you. I’m also not trying to rock their boat. But I do want to tell my story.

I used to fall into the former camp, then into the latter camp, and now that I’ve experienced two twin flame relationships, I’ve jumped into a new camp I never knew existed.

text:
Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural director/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.

It shouldn’t have to happen that way, though. It’s a bad shortcut to the divine archetypes.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. You’re already lost in the sauce once you start identifying with the way you see them, like she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me. I don’t mean it as a clinical diagnosis, but I do use it almost like one in my own life. If a woman says, “You’re such a great guy. Of course you have flaws like anyone, but I love you,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “You’re perfect, I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the BPD splitting happens, she can go from worshipping me to hating me, first in private and then in front of everybody. Suddenly she can find plenty of flaws, and all of them become evidence I was faking it all along. Sometimes she ends up accusing me of thinking I’m perfect, when she’s the one who used to say I was.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

For example, I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine.

text:
These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.

I’d rather be able to say “she’s cute” about a woman at the next table, and have my girlfriend say the same about some guy, without it turning into a fight. If only the serious crushes get mentioned, every mention turns into a confession, so people end up hiding all of them.

Lots of couples promise forever and nobody else. Look around at how many actually live that way. In a polyamorous relationship the boundaries might be more negotiable, but then somebody has to sit down and negotiate them, down to who gets to stay the night.

Polyamory can be dishonest too, like when someone who can’t get close to any one person dates four at once and calls it polyamory. Or when someone keeps cheating until they finally announce they’re poly, without necessarily doing the work on themselves that would make it ethical. If you can’t do monogamy, say so, since pretending can do more damage than an affair would have.

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it.

text:
These days, even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That’s why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can’t fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let’s see if I can fix that.”

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

The inner Magic 8 Ball came back YES, and I flipped off the mate-finding switch.

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once.

That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, speak your heart without hiding the insecurity behind anger, as in the above video I found on IG. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that’s fine, but don’t make the decision lightly, because it’s irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn’t. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.

I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.

For that to stay honest, I’d rather we could both mention attractions to other people casually, like saying “she’s cute” about a woman at the next table. If only the serious ones ever get mentioned, then any mention sounds serious, and people stop mentioning them at all.

Lots of couples promise forever and nobody else, and far fewer actually live that way, so a lot of them end up pretending. Polyamory leaves those rules open, so the boundaries have to be negotiated out loud, down to who gets to stay the night.

Polyamory can be dishonest too, though, like when someone who can’t get close to any one person dates four at once and calls it polyamory. Or when someone who can’t stop cheating just renames it polyamory, without necessarily doing the work on themselves that would make it ethical. Still, if you can’t do monogamy, it’s more honest to say so up front than to promise it and pretend, since pretending can do more damage than an affair would have.

I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it.
